mentl/ff163fd:
Three ticks took this from a seven-line subtraction crucible to three
lines:

  effect B { opb() -> Int }
  fn run(f) with Pure = f()
  fn main() = run(() => opb())

Pure is the empty row and the body calls an effectful callback. It
compiles.

A call to a function-typed parameter charges nothing to the enclosing
fn's inferred row, so the declared row is never checked against it. No
negation is involved, which is why the earlier framings kept sliding:
subtraction was a red herring, since diff_row provably populates the
absent set, and so was the annotation, since Pure shows it without one.

It corrects a peer Phase 1 records as closed.
hof-param-row-never-reaches-enclosing is recorded closed by the
signature keep-set, "publishes its param's row var in row and scheme
coherently". The scheme half is real and is exactly what
leak-higher-order, leak-hof-annotated and leak-hof-named-arg measure —
each puts its negation on the caller, where the instantiated scheme
delivers the callback's row. The row half is not: the enclosing fn's own
row stays Pure. Every HOF crucible in the battery tests the half that
works.

This is the negative-is-provable property failing at the shape most
likely to carry a real negation: a function taking a callback and
promising !Alloc, !IO or Pure. The caller is still charged through the
scheme, so simple programs are not miscompiled; the local claim is
false.

Banked as param-call-never-charges-the-declared-row, superseding the two
framings this arc filed and retracted. The three-line gate lands with
the fix.
mentl/ff440b8:
Narrowed the 5-minute sweep twice more, and the fix got much smaller than
the image cache I named an hour ago.

THE COST IS A FIXED FLOOR, not a function of the program. `fn main() = 7`
with NO imports costs 0.71s; + runtime/math 0.78s; + io + math + dsp/signal
0.95s. Every invocation pays ~0.71s regardless of what it references, and
149 x 0.71 = 106s of the sweep's 257s CPU is one prelude derived 149 times.

IT IS NOT INFERENCE. `mentl fmt` parses and renders without inferring and
costs 0.74s on the same fixture -- indistinguishable from check's 0.72s. The
floor is entirely pre-inference. The same wheel on the same program through
STDIN, no lib linked, is 0.040s. The difference is one thing: the path form
auto-links and PARSES THE PRELUDE.

SO THE FIX IS THE LAW THE WHEEL ALREADY LANDED, one layer up.
Construction-is-reachability made emission demand-driven: a name popping from
the frontier constructs its decl, a dead decl never constructs. THE LINK
NEVER GOT THAT LAW. It parses the whole prelude eagerly and then discovers
the program wanted none of it -- the same two-pass shape that arc deleted
from lower, every decl built up front and a second pass asking which
mattered. Demand-load the link and `fn main() = 7` parses nothing; the image
cache then sits on a floor that is already near zero instead of memoising
work that should never happen.

Split the peer: Hb.persist.module-image-cache keeps the caching half,
Hb.driver.link-is-reachability is this one, and it is the one to build first.

No time estimate accompanies this, and the previous one -- "a build, not an
afternoon" -- is withdrawn; it was a forbidden estimate used to pre-excuse
the work.

mentl/ff7ec2a:
Morgan asked "why the need for a wrapper at any point?" — testing it settled the
root. The -builtin-state repro with the use_each wrapper REMOVED (lambda created
directly in run's scope, the install site) PASSES (exit 42, no leak). So the
wrapper is load-bearing, not incidental, correcting the earlier "make_list state
init alone is the breaker" conclusion.

Root = a conjunction of two conditions:
  1. DEFECT: a Memory/Alloc effect in the handler's state init pollutes the
     residual row alongside the config-param user-effect var, severing its
     propagation into the installing fn's row (register_handler, infer.mn ~2627).
  2. TRIGGER: a wrapper fn (use_each = apply_each(lambda)) that creates the lambda
     OUTSIDE the handler-install scope, forcing its evidence to be FORWARDED
     through the wrapper's row. Lexical capture under the install reads the handler
     record locally and never consults the broken row, hiding the defect.

mn-higher-order-effect-builtin-no-wrapper (PASS) pins the wrapper as necessary.
The fix must keep this a PASS while flipping -builtin-state to 42.

mentl/ff88531:
THE Arc 2 self-miscompilation blocker. The compiler context tuple
(string_map, tag_map, fn_table, top_globals, type_env, vstack_base) was
accessed via ctx[i]. The Lux source `ctx[3]` lowers to LIndex which —
without type information showing ctx is a tuple — emits `call $list_index`.
The Rust VM's list_index opcode handles both List and Tuple natively,
so the bug was masked. In WASM, $list_index is a Lux function that reads
[count:i32][tag:i32][...] — for a tuple's raw [field0][field1]... layout,
that's a category error. ctx_globals returned random memory, every
handler-state LLet saw in_globals=false, every __hs_NAME emitted as
local.set, and lux4.wasm contained 110 UNRESOLVED references.

Fix: replace ctx_strings/tags/fns/globals/type_env/vstack_base with
tuple destructuring `let (s, _, _, _, _, _) = ctx; s`. Destructure
lowers to FieldAccess (is_tuple=true), which emits direct i32.load at
the correct offset. The structural answer was always one syntax change
away — ctx is a tuple; access it tuply.

Verified end-to-end: lux3 compiles counter.lux → 0 UNRESOLVED, valid
WASM. Stage2 Ouroboros completes (1:17:53), lux4.wasm validates
(425KB).

Root-caused via wasm-decompile of bootstrap/build/lux3.wasm:
  function ctx_globals(a:int, b:int):int {
    var ctx:int;
    return list_index(0, ctx, 3);
  }
The artifact named the bug; source-level guessing did not.
